rationale: The standard finite-coefficient definition is explicit in both sources. The item recasts it using zero-indexed finite lists, requires injective lists for a subset, and spells out the empty and zero-vector boundary cases.

The independence, inheritance, image, and finite-sum facts are standard consequences of the sourced finite-linear-combination treatment. The item bundles them with library-specific deletion, re-indexing, and zero-indexed concatenation formulas; its thirteen-step proof is a local derivation.

The source states and proves that a set is dependent exactly when one vector lies in the span of the others. The item adds the injective-list normal form for span and explicit empty/zero-singleton cases; its proof adapts the standard solve-for-a-nonzero-coefficient argument to that convention.

The source gives finite character and the union-of-a-chain independence assertion used in the Zorn argument. The item combines them and requires the chain to be nonempty so its finite-list base case has an available member; the detailed induction is local.

The source states that adjoining v to an independent S preserves independence exactly when v is outside span(S). The item adds the unchanged-span branch and the strict span inclusion, and adapts the usual coefficient argument to injective finite lists.

The source defines a Hamel basis through unique finite representations and immediately identifies the equivalent independent-spanning formulation. The item uses that formulation, adds ordered bases, subspace-relative bases, and the empty basis convention.

The source gives the unique representation theorem for a basis and its standard subtraction proof. The item strengthens the packaging to an iff for an arbitrary finite list and adds an exact formula for the span of its image.

Cambridge Proposition 1.1.4 states the same three-way equivalence for an arbitrary vector space: Hamel basis, maximal linearly independent set, and minimal spanning set. The item merely expands the inclusion-poset wording; its proof follows the standard maximal/minimal argument.

The source states the Steinitz exchange lemma with a finite spanning set, an independent set, the size inequality, and a complementary subset that still spans. The item expresses size through equinumerosity and derives finiteness rather than assuming it; the induction follows the sourced exchange strategy.

The standard finite-spanning-set bound appears in the source. The item states it for arbitrary independent subsets using equinumerosity and adds the exclusion of a countably infinite independent set; its proof is a local corollary of the preceding exchange theorem.

The source proves invariance of the length of finite bases. The item also says that once one finite basis exists every basis is finite, and it uses natural-number equinumerosity instead of list length; the two-bound argument is locally assembled.

Both sources define finite dimension as the size of a basis. The item adopts the convention that dim is undefined, rather than cardinal- or infinity-valued, for spaces without a finite basis and explicitly includes dimension zero.

Colorado Theorem 1.15 gives I subset B subset S for an independent I inside a spanning S and proves it by Zorn. The source states the nonzero-space version; the item includes the zero space and makes the Axiom of Choice hypothesis explicit, while retaining the same proof.

Colorado Theorem 1.15 states that every spanning set contains a basis. The item includes the zero-space boundary and explicitly carries the AC dependency; its proof is the local one-line specialization with the empty independent set.

Cambridge Theorem 1.1.6 states exactly that every vector space has a Hamel basis. The item's zero-space sentence only identifies the theorem's boundary instance; the supplied proof is a local application of the preceding extension theorem.

Cambridge Example 1.1.7 gives the standard basis of K^n. The item adds pointwise evaluation of arbitrary finite sums, the coordinate formula, the dimension conclusion, zero-based indices, and n=0; its inductive proof is local.

The sources give the subspace dimension bound, equality only for the whole finite-dimensional space, and finite basis extension. The item bundles these with an explicit no-choice claim and uses a bespoke greatest-attainable-size argument.

Colorado Corollary 1.16 states for an arbitrary subspace S of V that a subspace T exists with V=S direct-sum T. The item makes the inherited AC hypothesis explicit; its basis-extension proof is the standard sourced construction.

The source assumes only that U and W are finite-dimensional and gives dim(U+W)=dim U+dim W-dim(U intersection W). The item uses the subtraction-free equivalent equality, states intersection finiteness and boundary cases, and adapts the standard compatible-bases proof.

The source states additivity of dimension for a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional subspaces. The item reformulates it for a natural-number-indexed family, includes n=0 and n=2, and proves it by a local induction from the two-subspace formula.

The exact three-basis witness with x=(1,2), v_0=(1,1), and v_1=(1,0) is a locally designed worked example rather than a recoverable quoted construction. Direct substitution gives coordinate lists (1,2), (2,1), and (2,-1), and the determinant of the nonstandard basis matrix is -1, so every assertion is immediately verified.

Cambridge Example 1.1.7(ii) defines c00 as the eventually zero sequences over K and states that the unit sequences form a basis. The item adds ambient-subspace, bijection, and no-finite-basis clauses and supplies its own pointwise verification.

The source states that R has a basis over Q and that its Q-dimension is uncountable. The item expands the canonical embedding and restriction-of-scalars bookkeeping and proves non-finiteness from countability of finite powers of Q.

Cambridge Example 1.1.7 contrasts the independent unit sequences with a sequence space they do not span. The item uses all F-valued families, identifies the span as the eventually zero subspace, and chooses the constant-one family as an explicit witness.

The source uses the standard dependent spanning set {e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2}. The item generalizes it to every field, verifies all three two-element subsets are bases, and treats characteristic two explicitly.

The source asks for a proper subspace of the eventually zero sequence space having an equinumerous basis. The item supplies the concrete shift subspace span{e_k:k>=1}, its successor bijection, and a pointwise proof that e_0 is excluded.

The source explicitly says that the usual three lines in F^2 refute the exact three-subspace inclusion-exclusion claim. The item writes the three lines as spans of e_0, e_1, and e_0+e_1 over an arbitrary field and verifies every dimension.

Hefferon's answer gives two independent subsets of R^2 whose union is dependent and records the general union criterion. The item uses the same e_0,e_1,e_0+e_1 pattern over an arbitrary field and provides a direct singleton-and-union refutation.
